newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says no change in unification policy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says no change in unification policy.

text.p: Taiwan on Thursday brushed off charges by rival China that it was seeking independence from the communist mainland, saying its desire for eventual unification had not changed.

"The Chinese communists should not have worried that we would pursue a pro-independence policy. Their concern is unnecessary," said Jan Jyh-horng, a department director of the cabinet-level Mainland Affairs Council.
His comment came after a warning on Wednesday by Beijing's official Xinhua news agency that Taiwan would meet disaster if it insisted on "splitting" from the motherland.

In a commentary on the eve of the second anniversary of a 1995 reconciliation call by Chinese President Jiang Zemin, the agency said Taiwan had failed to answer Jiang's appeal and had actively sought to split Taiwan from China.
Beijing, which views Taiwan as a rebel province, refuses to rule out the use of force to recover the island if Taipei declares independence.
In his 1995 speech, Jiang called for an end to hostilities and the opening of direct trade links.
Jan said Taiwan's political reforms, including free speech and removal of the draconian sedition statute instituted to silence dissidents, were not intended to lead to independence.

"In the process of reforms, the Chinese communists have repeatedly voiced its concerns and criticism, but their worries have all been proven unnecessary," he said. "We have never changed our unification policy.
"Unification between the two sides of the Taiwan Strait is a long-term goal, which we are not going to drop," he added.

But an opinion poll conducted by the local United Daily News showed that independence from China was gaining support among Taiwan people, after two years in which Taipei's relations with Beijing had turned sour.
The poll showed that 34 percent of 1,014 respondents supported full independence from China, up from 24 percent in February 1995.
The number advocating independence was just under the 37 percent supporting unification with the mainland.
Beijing staged war games near Taiwan between August 1995 and March 1996 to try to intimidate the island over what it perceived as a growing trend towards independence.
It suspended semi-official talks with Taiwan after Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui visited the United States in June 1995 in a trip it saw as an attempt to promote independence.
